items.label: Why Git matters for security work

slots.title: Why Git matters for security work

body.html:
• Track every change to exploit code, PoCs, and tool configs — reproducibility matters when a technique needs to be re-run or re-audited
  • Roll back a broken payload or config instantly instead of hand-restoring
  • Collaborate on CTF writeups and internal tooling without emailing zip files
  • Full history = an audit trail: who changed what, when, and why
  • Every exercise and lab in this course is submitted via Git

• Working directory — the files you're actually editing
  • Staging area (index) — a holding area for changes you're about to commit
  • Repository (.git) — the committed history, stored as snapshots

A commit moves a snapshot of the staged files from the staging area into the repository, permanently.

slots.title: Local vs. remote, snapshots not diffs

body.html:
• Every clone is a full copy of the repository — history included, no server round-trip needed to inspect it
  • The .git/ folder holds the entire database: objects, refs, config
  • Git stores each commit as a snapshot of the whole tree (not a diff) — deleted/unchanged files are just re-referenced, so this is cheap
  • A remote (e.g. origin) is just another repository you sync with — GitHub/GitLab are remotes, not "the real thing"

git init                # create a new repo
git clone <url>        # copy an existing repo
git status               # what changed?
git add <file>          # stage changes
git commit -m "msg"      # snapshot staged changes
git log --oneline        # view history

git branch                    # list branches
git branch <name>            # create a branch
git switch <name>            # move to it
git switch -c <name>         # create + switch

Branch per exercise, per tool, per exploit variant — never develop directly on main. A broken branch never breaks the working version.

git switch main
git merge <branch>
  • Fast-forward — main hasn't moved, Git just slides the pointer forward
  • Merge commit — both branches moved, Git creates a commit with two parents
  • Conflict — same lines changed on both sides; Git marks <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> in the file for you to resolve by hand, then git add + git commit

git remote -v                 # list remotes
git push origin <branch>
git fetch origin              # download, don't merge
git pull origin <branch>      # fetch + merge

origin is your remote; upstream is convention for the original repo you forked from.

# .gitignore
.env
*.pem
*.key
credentials.json
id_rsa*

Anything matched here is never staged, never committed. In security work this is non-negotiable: API keys, private keys, target credentials, and client data must never enter Git history.

• Committing a secret before adding it to .gitignore — the file is already in history, ignoring it now does nothing
  • History exposure — a public repo's full commit history is downloadable, including anything ever committed and later "deleted"
  • Removing a leaked secret requires rewriting history (git filter-repo / BFG) and rotating the credential — assume it's compromised the moment it's pushed
  • Force-pushing over shared branches, wiping teammates' work
